excerpts:
# Understanding Crypto Gas Fees: A Beginner’s Guide to Ethereum
On April 7, the average Ethereum gas price printed at around 0.052 [gwei](https://plisio.net/crypto/gwei) , one of the quietest readings the network has ever logged. A plain transfer went through for a few cents. Wind back a year on the same chain and the same send could have cost five dollars in the middle of a busy afternoon.

...

## How Ethereum Gas Fees Work: Gas Price, Gas Limit, Gwei
Every fee on the Ethereum mainnet is paid in ether. That stays true even if you are sending a dollar-pegged token like USDC or a wrapped version of bitcoin. The network only knows one currency for gas, and that currency is ether.

...

## Base Fee, Priority Fee, and the Transaction Fee Formula
A quick example. You want to send 0.5 ETH to a friend on a quiet afternoon. Gas used is 21,000. Base fee is 4 gwei. You tip 1 gwei. The math works out to 21,000 × (4 + 1) = 105,000 gwei, or 0.000105 ETH. At $3,500 per ether, that is roughly $0.37. Drop the same transfer into a congested NFT mint and the base might jump to 80 gwei plus a 10 gwei tip, dragging the cost past $6. Same formula. Very different inputs.

...

## Why Your ETH Gas Fee Changes With Network Congestion
The trade-off is straightforward. Until Layer 2 rollups fully absorb routine activity, Ethereum users on mainnet keep feeling price pressure during peak times. That absorption is now well underway. The Ethereum base layer in early 2026 looks quieter than it has since 2019.

...

## Gas Used, Gas Costs, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine
The table below shows what that tax looks like in practice, using live 2026 data and an ether price around $3,500.

...

Two things jump out. First, the gap between simple and complex transactions is real. A contract deployment can cost 20 to 30 times more than a transfer at the same gas price. Second, the 50 gwei column looks painful, but in 2026 that only shows up during rare spikes. The 4 gwei column is closer to the everyday experience since Fusaka.

...

## Layer 2 Rollups: Use Eth Gas Without the Pain
Layer 2 rollups are the reason ethereum gas fees feel so different in 2026. A rollup is a separate chain that executes transactions off the mainnet, then posts a compressed proof back to Ethereum. Users get Ethereum-grade security without Ethereum-level fees.

...

## Using a Gas Tracker to Time Your Transactions Right
These gas fee trackers are the most used options in 2026, each giving a gas price in real time:

...

## How to Lower Your ETH Gas Fee in Practice Today
**1. Move to a Layer 2.** This is the single biggest change you can make. Bridging ETH or stablecoins once to Base, Arbitrum, or Optimism unlocks fees a hundred times smaller than the mainnet. The saved gas usually pays off the bridging fee within a handful of transactions.

...

## Historical Gas Trends After the Ethereum 2.0 Merge
The current era started in 2024 and is still running. Dencun kicked it off by giving rollups cheap blob storage. Pectra turned the blob dials up. Fusaka finished the job late last year. The average ethereum gas price in April 2026 sits roughly 90% below where it was a year earlier, and L2 fees dropped even more.

...

## The Bottom Line on Crypto Gas Fees
If you are new to this in 2026, the playbook is shorter than it looks. Keep a little ether in your crypto wallet for things that really need Ethereum mainnet. Move routine activity to a Layer 2 like Base, Arbitrum, or Optimism. For stablecoin payments across borders, Solana, Polygon, or TRON with rented energy usually win on cost. Glance at a gas tracker before anything expensive. Tweak the priority fee instead of guessing at raw gas prices.

...

Gas fees will keep moving. That is what a blockchain priced by supply and demand for block space does for a living. But the worst mainnet pain sits firmly in the pre-rollup era, and the next billion users of the ethereum ecosystem will probably never see 100 gwei unless they go digging for it on purpose.

excerpts:
# Protocol Update 001 – Scale L1
## TL;DR
* [Marius van der Wijden](https://github.com/MariusVanDerWijden) joined Ansgar Dietrichs and Tim Beiko to co-lead Scale L1
* Mainnet’s gas limit increased to 45M post- [Berlinterop](https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/06/19/checkpoint-4) , a first step on the road to 100M gas and beyond
* All major execution layer clients shipped [Pre-Merge History Expiry](https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/07/08/partial-history-exp) , significantly reducing node disk usage

...

## Towards a 100M Mainnet Gas Limit
Our immediate goal is safely scaling Ethereum’s mainnet gas limit to 100M per block. [Parithosh Jayanthi](https://github.com/parithosh) , closely supported by Nethermind's PerfNet team, is leading our work getting through [each incremental increase](https://ethpandaops.io/posts/gaslimit-scaling/) .
At the recent [Berlinterop event](https://blog.ethereum.org/2025/06/19/checkpoint-4) , client teams significantly improved their worst-case performance benchmarks, enabling the recent increase to 45M gas --- a first step on the path toward 100M gas and beyond!
Additionally, client hardening has become an integral part of the 100M Gas initiative. The Pectra upgrade rollout highlighted several issues caused by network instability. It is paramount to ensure clients remain robust as throughput increases, even if the network temporarily loses finality.

...

## Benchmarking & Pricing
An ongoing challenge in scaling Ethereum is aligning the gas costs of EVM operations with their computational overhead. The performance of worst-case edge cases currently limits network throughput.
By improving benchmarking infrastructure and repricing operations that can't be optimized by clients, we can make block execution times more consistent. If we close the gap between the worst and average case blocks, we can then raise the gas limit commensurately.

...

In parallel, [Carlos Pérez](https://github.com/cperezz) spearheads [Bloatnet](https://cperezz.github.io/bloatnet-website/index.html) : an initiative aimed at benchmarking and optimizing state performance. This involves testing node performance under conditions with state sizes double the current mainnet and gas limits reaching 100–150M, to directly inform both repricings and client optimizations.

## How gas fees work
### Why Layer 2 Fees Are Lower
Layer 2 networks process transactions off Ethereum mainnet and post compressed batches of data back as proofs. By amortising Ethereum security costs across many transactions, the per-transaction cost falls dramatically. Optimistic rollups (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) use fraud proofs; zero-knowledge rollups (Linea, Scroll) use cryptographic validity proofs.

...

### Timing and Trend Indicators
The base fee on Ethereum adjusts block by block. When blocks are more than 50 per cent full, the base fee rises; when they are less than 50 per cent full, it falls. For Ethereum mainnet, fees tend to be lower during off-peak UTC hours and at weekends when on-chain activity is reduced.

...

## External references and documentation
EIP-4844: Shard Blob Transactions (Proto-Danksharding)
Introduces blob-carrying transactions that provide Layer 2 networks with a cheaper data availability channel, significantly reducing the cost of posting batches to Ethereum mainnet.

...

Etherscan's public gas tracker showing live Ethereum mainnet base fee, priority fee recommendations, and historical gas price charts. Useful for cross-referencing the data on this page.
[Read source](https://etherscan.io/gastracker)

...

## Frequently asked questions
As of 19 October 2026, 16:02 UTC, among the 10 networks online, Scroll has the lowest token swap cost at $0.00005765 per swap, against $0.1034 on Ethereum mainnet. Layer 2 networks typically record 90 to 99 per cent lower fees than Ethereum mainnet. These figures change block by block.

...

As of 19 October 2026, 16:02 UTC, the Ethereum mainnet gas price is 0.20 gwei (base fee 0.19 gwei). At the average fee tier a simple ETH transfer costs about $0.0145, a token swap about $0.1034 and an NFT mint about $0.0586, using an ETH price of $2,400.

...

Layer 2 networks process transactions off the Ethereum mainnet and post compressed batches of transaction data back to Ethereum as proof, either as optimistic rollup fraud proofs (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base) or zero-knowledge validity proofs (Linea, Scroll). By batching many transactions into a single Ethereum data submission, the per-transaction cost of Ethereum security falls dramatically.

...

Network demand drives the base fee. For Ethereum mainnet, the base fee tends to be lower during off-peak hours in UTC, broadly late at night and into early morning in European time zones, and at weekends when trading activity and automated protocol interactions are generally reduced. Layer 2 fee patterns broadly follow mainnet, though they can also be influenced by the cost of posting batches to Ethereum.
